title: SQL vs NoSQL
short: Strict tables you can join, or simple records that spread out.
what: A SQL (relational) database keeps data in tables with fixed columns, links tables with joins, and runs a group of changes all or nothing (a transaction). NoSQL databases (key-value, document, wide-column) give up some of that to make one kind of access very fast and easy to spread over many machines.
analogy: SQL is a set of strict spreadsheets that reference each other. NoSQL is a wall of labelled folders: grab one folder by its label and everything about that thing is inside.

frames.say: A shop stores users and orders. In a SQL database each is a table with fixed columns. orders.user_id points to a row in users.
To show Ana's orders with her name, one query joins the two tables. The database matches the rows for you.
Checkout must charge Ana and create her order. A transaction makes both happen or neither. SQL databases are built for this.
Now carts: 50,000 updates a second, always read by user, never joined. A key-value store gives you one key and one record.
The store spreads keys over many machines by itself. Need more speed? Add a node. Each read touches one node.
The trade-off: ask it 'which carts hold the red mug?' and there is no join or query for that. You would read every cart.
Most real systems use both: SQL for users, orders and money; NoSQL for carts, sessions and feeds. Pick by how you read the data.

when: Data has relations and you query it in many ways (SQL)
Money or stock counts must be exact (SQL)
Huge write volume, always read by one key (NoSQL)
Record shape changes often or differs per record (document store)
python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT)")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER, user_id INTEGER, total REAL)")
db.execute("INSERT INTO users VALUES (42, 'Ana')")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (?, 42, ?)", [(1, 19.5), (2, 5.0)])
rows = db.execute("SELECT name, SUM(total) FROM users JOIN orders ON orders.user_id = users.id GROUP BY name")
print("SQL join:", rows.fetchall())

carts = {"cart:ana": {"items": ["mug", "tea"], "updated": "12:01"}}   # NoSQL style: one key, one record
print("NoSQL get:", carts["cart:ana"]["items"])
cost: built into most NoSQL; manual sharding for SQL
watch: NoSQL is not faster in general; it is fast for the one access pattern you designed it for.
Start with SQL when data has relations or money involved; one machine goes further than people think.
NoSQL often stores the same data twice, and you must keep the copies in sync yourself.
